doc.title: Panama Francis interviewed by Michael Woods, Los Angeles, California, September 1, 1995

chapter: Drumming concepts and jazz as a word
title: Tuning the drums and playing for the dancers
summary: He tunes the bass drum to G with tympani heads to blend with the bass, defends the bass drum, and plays for the one person tapping a foot.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Early drum kits and the gear drummers used

blocks.x: Tell us about the drums as a musical instrument. How do you get different tones and sounds out the drums?
Because it’s not just a percussion instrument.
It is a percussion instrument. That’s what it is.
Yes but you get many different tone colors out of it.

Well I mean you tune it up. You very seldom see me without this [drum key]. I’ve always got it. So I tune up the drums. And I tune them to different sounds. And like with my bass drum, up until in recent years, I used tympani heads on the bass drum. So I used to tune my bass drum to G so it could blend with the bass fiddle. And see they don’t do that anymore. The guys, I don’t know. Something happened somewhere down the line that it’s, you know, it’s been changed. And they you know speak about, well you don’t have to play any bass drum, you just use the bass drum to accent. That’s crap. The bass drum is very important. But that’s the reason why when I play, I look out in that audience, and if I don’t see nobody doing, well patting their foot or something, then I ain’t swinging. I’m not swinging. Something is missing. I’m not getting to them. But if I see one person out there patting their foot or shaking their head, I play for them. Forget about the other people, I’ll play for that one person. Because that’s where my inspiration comes from. And I love to watch people dance, because that really inspires me, to watch people dance.
